item.title: Middle Powers and Transformative AI: A request for proposals
item.description:
Published on September 23, 2026 7:55 PM GMT

Today, we are launching a request for proposals on AI policy in middle powers, with $10M (and potentially more) of funding available. Apply at middlepowers.ai by October 23.

I think that most countries are on track to become increasingly irrelevant to the future of technology, the economy, and geopolitics. The US and China, along with perhaps a few countries with key roles in the chip supply chain and data center buildout, will hold all the cards. The rest of the world will be bystanders, or at best passengers on the great train of history, unable to affect the destination. I hope that middle powers can help ensure AI is developed for the benefit of all of humanity.

Having one country, or even one company, make many of the key decisions shaping the future of humanity would be an extreme concentration of power. Even if decision-makers are well-intentioned, they may miss considerations that would have been caught by stronger checks and balances from more actors being involved. And given the propensity of power to corrupt, we can reasonably worry about the judgement and values of whoever ends up calling the shots. AI development is more likely to be safe, secure, and broadly beneficial if it is shaped by a wider range of democratic countries.

Concretely, we think middle powers need to:

  1. Recognize the stakes. Treat transformative AI as the top strategic, economic, and national security priority it is, and build the political will and institutional capacity to act.
  2. Build leverage. Maintain and strengthen their positions in the data center buildout,[1] semiconductor supply chain, and downstream industrial AI applications.
  3. Use that leverage well. Work out what to ask for (access to frontier systems, transparency into what frontier developers are building, enforceable safety requirements, etc.), coordinate with other middle powers, and use their leverage to partner with great powers on securing these outcomes.
  4. Help the great powers coordinate. Build the verification technology, institutions, and diplomatic capacity that make agreements between great powers more likely and more robust.

This won’t be easy. It may not even be possible on the shortest timelines. But it is imperative that middle powers use what influence they have while they can, and build leverage to deploy later. It was heartening to see a coalition of middle powers calling for stronger safeguards to keep AI under human control at the UN this week.

To help you get started we have listed 16 categories of projects we would be excited to fund, including work on data centers, chip supply chains, building political will, diplomacy, field building, evaluation and verification, and more. We also include a reading list for getting up to speed if you want to contribute but aren’t that familiar with past work.

If you are a researcher or a writer, a builder or a convener, a dreamer or a doer, we look forward to hearing from you!

  1. ^

    What about the worry that building more data centers accelerates AI progress and so is bad? I would be happy to see more modelling on this, but my understanding (based on some research and talking to relevant people) is that by far the greatest bottleneck on the compute buildout is chip manufacturing. There are no stacks of GPUs waiting for a data center to house them, and there won’t be anytime soon. There will be some small effect on the margin where making data centers cheaper and easier to build makes that business slightly more profitable, allowing hyperscalers to pay slightly more for chips, allowing semiconductor companies to invest slightly more in capex. But this effect seems small, and so a good approximation is that building a data center in one place causes one fewer data center to be built elsewhere.

item.title: The vegan trap: are we making animal advocacy harder than it needs to be?
item.description:
Published on September 24, 2026 7:48 AM GMT

note: crosspost from my substack

As a vegan for almost thirty years, I’ve long had second thoughts about how effective veganism is for helping animals. I am not alone in this. Recently others have expressed doubts about veganism (see for instance here, here, here, here, or here)

To be sure, veganism has its uses. In essence, veganism is about boycotting animal products - which are almost invariably the products of suffering and exploitation. The hope is that with enough people participating in this boycott, we’ll have an impact on demand, and fewer - ultimately no - animals would be used for food (or other purposes). Veganism also has a signalling function: we show that we don’t participate in animal cruelty because we think it’s wrong. And veganism provides our movement with an identity, which can help with internal cohesion. When a vegan meets another vegan, they know that they “get it”. No conversation is necessary. They have arrived at the same place as we have. They’re one of us. We understand each other. And we’ll feel betrayed and take it personally when others give up on veganism.

Vegans, no doubt, deserve respect. It’s not easy to be vegan in this world and it requires commitment. I have the utmost respect for vegans and still generally consider them “my people”. And no worries, I’m continuing to be vegan, and so should you.

The number of vegans is hardly growing.

But veganism also has quite a few disadvantages and challenges. Before I get into these, let me add that in the thirty years I’ve been into animal activism, I’ve gotten a lot of criticism from vegans, because I’ve always criticized vegan policing and purity politics. I think those are not useful (see below). To say this is to invite scapegoating, bullying and gatekeeping upon oneself - and sometimes all of this can get quite nasty (here’s an example of a person who’s been disingenuously attacking me for many years). It doesn’t bode well for our movement that people who have worked for the animals for decades still have to explain their intentions.

Over the years, I’ve often heard this elegant-sounding theory of change: if every vegan made one other person vegan in one year and those new vegans would do the same, then in five or six years a country could be vegan, starting from a very small base of 1%. It sounds feasible. It’s actually hard to think of why it would not work. But of course it doesn’t. The number of vegans is not increasing. And it’s not just being vegan that’s hard. Staying vegan is also hard. Surveys show that at any given moment there are more ex-vegans than vegans.

Many organizations have therefore moved on from personal vegan outreach to institutional change, welfare reforms, reduction asks, and climate and health messaging. Still, veganism is very much a part of our DNA as a movement. Which is why I’m addressing it.

Veganism has many challenges and downsides

  • It can become a very strong in-group identity, which, like I said, is an advantage to a point, but it means that it becomes harder for other people to join us.
  • Veganism may become the price of entry to our “club”. If somebody’s not vegan, some animal activists may wonder if they belong among us. This dynamic makes us quite unique as a movement, and I can’t think of similar dynamics in other movements. Imagine the environmental movement: you won’t be shown the door if you show up at a protest with a petrol car. Few other movements have strict requirements and black-and-white rules like the animal rights movement often has.
  • Veganism may imply an over-focus on individual change and personal responsibility at the cost of activism or political engagement. Maybe you heard that the concept of the personal carbon footprint was developed by an advertising agency, Ogilvy, for British Petroleum. The idea was to show people what they were personally responsible for in terms of climate impact, and thus take some of the focus and blame away from the fossil fuel companies.
  • Veganism can also be a hindrance to collaboration. I remember, in my time when I was working in an organization, how now and then we said no to certain opportunities where we could amplify our message. Some party with a broad reach would want to create and spread a recipe booklet with us, but they wanted some non-vegan recipes in it. So we said no - a missed opportunity based on principles.
  • Veganism can become an end in itself, the only thing that matters. And being vegan may give one a moral licence not to do more. One may think: I’m vegan, I’m doing my part.
  • Veganism may push us to communicate ineffectively: a representative of an animal organization, speaking in public, may know that pragmatically it’s better to be more moderate, but may fear the backlash from vegans - and thus say things that are not optimal for the public at large.
  • Finally, veganism is a very demanding and unattractive concept, and if we’re asking people to go vegan, we’re putting the bar very high. Veganism seems daunting and difficult, and people doubt that it’s healthy. People dislike vegans. And once you’re vegan it may be hard to keep up because of health, social and other challenges, compassion fatigue, and so on.

Creating barriers

One of the main problems I see is that if someone is vegan, this makes that person automatically seem quite different from non-vegans, as if we’re talking about different kinds of people, with different identities. Veganism, in this sense, draws up a wall and makes it harder to speak with others.

The basic dynamic at work is what we call do-gooder derogation. When somebody does something good, it often makes another person feel bad about themselves because the other is not doing that good thing. I’ve written in another post about Anthony Robbins saying that our universal fear is to not be enough, to not be good or smart enough. Vegans, by being vegan, unintentionally tell other people who are not vegan that they’re not good enough. That, at least, is how it’s often perceived, and that is what creates a wall and stops conversation and relationships. Do-gooder derogation means that the non-vegan is going to derogate the vegan (the do-gooder). They’re going to attack and ridicule them out of self-defense, and the chances that the non-vegan will change their behaviour get smaller.

What if we had never invented veganism?

This is a question I’ve started to ask myself over the last few years. What if Donald Watson had never come up with the concept in 1944? It seems absurd to want to help animals, farmed animals in particular, and all the while not completely avoiding their consumption.

It’s not a perfect comparison but the anti-slavery abolitionists had a concept very similar to veganism: the so-called Free Produce Movement. Its adherents were people who boycotted any products from slavery (such as sugar, tobacco or cotton). They even had their own stores, similar to vegan stores. This concept, however, was discussed and criticized a lot and, after some time, was let go of. It was never a major thing in the abolitionist movement. Abolitionists thought the bar was too high and instead focused on political, societal, and institutional change rather than individual purity and individual ethical behaviour.

Then what do we do?

First: let go of the insistence on purity - at least by other people. Be as pure as you want, but don’t put the bar too high for others. The requirement to be vegan always, everywhere, in every situation is ineffective because it turns people off. It’s also impossible, because there are all kinds of animal ingredients in our food, in our life, in our practices. It can be unnecessary - for instance, if now and then one eats animal products from a dumpster, one has no impact on demand. Finally, it’s insufficient, because vegan products might still be detrimental for animals, the planet or other people.

I’d say we’d be more successful if we saw veganism as a 98% thing rather than a 100% thing. Melanie Joy talks about being “as vegan as possible.” Veganish is another term we could use. Again, do what you want, just don’t expect purity from others, and certainly don’t exclude them if their definition of veganism is not sufficiently close to yours. You’ll only make the vegan club smaller.

Secondly, we can use other asks. We can talk about reduction, about vegetarianism. We can launch concepts like “home veganism” (eating vegan at home, not so strict outside) or “weekday veganism”. There are different ways to make it easier to get people to take the first step.

Thirdly, rather than focus on personal diet change, we should go more institutional, structural, political. Rather than asking lifestyle changes from people, we can ask them to help us campaign, vote, donate and thus contribute to systemic change. Chris Bryant from Bryant Research talks about Vegan 2.0, where veganism is about avoiding the most horrible forms of animal suffering and being active against them.

This is actually reflected in the original rules of the Vegan Society. Back in 1944 they set up an associate, so a member, who “makes no promise as to behaviour, but declares himself in agreement with the object”.

The vegan trap

Suppose I was able to prove to you (obviously I am not), without a shadow of a doubt, that our use of the concept of veganism is detrimental for animals. Would we change?

I don’t think so - because vegans are in what I call the vegan trap. We are, I think, to some extent the hostages of our ideals and of our movement. They make us do or avoid things out of principle, out of good intentions - and this is not always the best thing for animals.

The way we are trapped is that we cannot easily change ourselves. We cannot choose not to be vegan, even for a moment, even if it would be pragmatic to do so. We can’t stop believing that moral persuasion works - even if we see that veganism still hasn’t made a dent in animal products consumption. Veganism is also part of who we are, part of our identity. We can’t shake it. And we are very uncomfortable with inconsistencies: it doesn’t feel good to make exceptions. We want to do the 100%.

Many of us also have a hard time stopping trying to influence others from going vegan. Imagine a non-vegan turns up at a vegan potluck. What do vegans do? They zoom in on their new “target” and will try to convert them, for better or for worse. Because it’s what we believe in.

Lastly, part of the vegan trap is also the group pressure. Even if we think it might be wiser to do or say this or that, the rest of the group might push us back in line.

 

The vegan trap - created by Gemini AI

We need more non-vegans

Often, vegans’ attitudes toward vegans and non-vegans come down to something like this: a vegan can do nothing wrong; a non-vegan can do nothing right. We don’t criticize the vegan who never leaves his house and doesn’t do any influencing. We do criticize a non-vegan advocate for animals.

Vegans are one percent of the population. It will be difficult, if not impossible, to change things for animals with this small group alone. Fortunately, there are many more people who can theoretically help animals - including farmed animals - than there are vegans. There are many more people who are in favour of the closing of slaughterhouses than there are vegans. There are many people who are not vegan but have money to help animals. Take Dustin Moskovitz, a co-founder of Facebook. With his fund, Coefficient Giving, he’s the biggest funder of animal welfare in the world. But he’s not vegan.

This is not all. Non-vegans may be better advocates sometimes. They’re less limited by our rules - they’re not in the vegan trap. They can speak more freely. We are often beholden to our orthodoxy and cannot always bring the best and most suitable message. They are often less threatening and more relatable, so they might be better messengers for animals.

A simple point about communication: it consists of what is said, how it is said, and who says it. Who is the messenger? Who is talking to whom? We know from research, at least from this one study, that messages by non-vegans about the same thing are perceived as less threatening than messages by vegans. Non-vegans can be better spokespeople for our cause, sometimes.

Here’s an example. Days Without Meat (Dagen Zonder Vlees) was an extremely successful vegetarian campaign in Belgium, asking people to go vegetarian or reduce meat consumption during the period of Lent (the 40 days before Easter). At some point over 100,000 people actively participated, in a small country like Belgium, and everyone knew about it. This campaign was organized by a female student who was not vegan or even vegetarian. But I think the effect was that the people who participated didn’t have the impression that there was some vegan from on high telling others what to do. Instead, the audience was in the same boat as the campaigners, meaning they felt a lot less judged. (Note: in a newspaper interview, this young woman said she never said no to a good chicken curry. The fact that I cursed inwardly when I read that, shows that I, too, am in the vegan trap).

Enlisting non-vegans’ help for animals

How do we reach these non-vegans and get them to help animals? We need to do at least three things.

  1. We need to attract them. Show them that they are capable of helping, even if they’re not vegan. One example comes from Aaron Boddy, from Ambitious Impact. He is very committed to animals, but posted this on his LinkedIn: “I ran an animal charity and I eat dairy.” Some people objected, but I think it’s definitely worth trying to avoid people thinking that they can’t participate because they’re not vegan.
  2. We need to allow them to be among us. Here is a little thought experiment. Imagine a vegan pride parade. Who is welcome to be there? Are non-vegans welcome? I don’t think that at the moment they are as welcome as straight people are at a Pride parade, but they definitely should be.
  3. We need to keep them, and with this, I think I mean: “keep them non-vegan”. Often when some vegans will make the case for including non-vegans, they’ll say that these people will turn vegan anyway by being among us. That may be true in many cases, but I’m not sure if it’s actually the best outcome. Maybe some non-vegans should STAY non-vegan - at least for quite some time - to help increase the heterogeneity of our group, so that we can attract more people still. If every non-vegan joining goes vegan tomorrow, we won’t have increased our recruiting power.

All of the above are things for your consideration, and I’m 100% sure of exactly none of it. These are ideas that go against the vegan grain, but I believe as people who take up the plight of beings who can’t fight for themselves, that we keep asking hard questions - and still trust each other to have the best of intentions.

  2. We need to allow them to be among us. Here is a little thought experiment. Imagine a vegan pride parade. Who is welcome to be there? Are non-vegans welcome? I don’t think that at the moment they are as welcome as straight people are at a Pride parade, but they definitely should be.
  3. We need to keep them, and with this, I think I mean: “keep them non-vegan”. Often when some vegans will make the case for including non-vegans, they’ll say that these people will turn vegan anyway by being among us. Maybe some non-vegans should STAY non-vegan - at least for quite some time - to help increase the heterogeneity of our group, so that we can attract more people still. If every non-vegan joining goes vegan tomorrow, we won’t have increased our recruiting power.

All of the above are things for your consideration, and I’m 100% sure of exactly none of it. These are ideas that go against the vegan grain, but I believe as people who take up the plight of beings who can’t fight for themselves, that we keep asking hard questions - and still trust each other to have the best of intentions.

item.title: Why I’m optimistic about cultivated meat (and a suggestion for the frontier labs)
item.description:
Published on September 24, 2026 7:55 PM GMT

In my first “Meat Matters” substack, I wrote that despite some recent popular press obituaries, I remain optimistic about the scientific viability of cultivated meat, and I spelled out why. 

Here’s the executive summary: 

In less than a decade, costs have fallen by orders of magnitude, government funding and scientific progress have surged, and multiple companies report that they are within striking distance of price parity. In short: The science and engineering challenges will not require inconceivably difficult breakthroughs or AGI, and of the dozens of cultivated meat scientists and engineers I spoke with for my new book Meat, all of them are optimistic about our path forward.

Zak Weston from Food System Innovations (FSI) works on market shaping for FSI and has personally reviewed techno-economic analyses from five different cultivated meat companies. He says that those analyses show “that at current cell line and media performance, if produced in commercial-scale facilities, they could reach cost parity or cost advantage compared to their animal meat benchmark.”

In Zak's view (and mine), “the technological progress over the past few years has been remarkable.”

Click here to read the full piece, and if you'd like to receive a monthly dose of optimism and urgency related to alternative meats, please subscribe. 

An ITN project for Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s life sciences divisions (and Google DeepMind)

Although I'm optimistic about getting cultivated meat to price parity with the full range of conventional meats, I don't think it's going to be easy, and I do think there’s a good chance that we could fail. 

If we fail, though, it will be because we didn't bring the will, not because the scientific and engineering challenges were insurmountable. 

It’s also worth noting that every second, the world slaughters 2,800 land animals and 4,100 farmed fin fish. That number has been going up every single year since FAO started measuring, in 1961. 

So even if solving cultivated meat will happen eventually, solving it quicker matters. A lot.

Our current path forward involves two vectors: 

  1. startups, which are doing incredibly well, especially considering how little has been spent on the project; right now is a great time to invest, since the top startups in cultivated meat are drastically undervalued.
  2. open access science, which is making great progress, especially considering the relative dearth of resources. 

With the budgets, expertise, and connections of the frontier labs, the fundamental science and engineering roadmap for cheap cultivated meat could be created and then handed to the world. 

With some additional resources, the labs could accelerate the current start-ups and launch new ones, creating a robust cultivated meat industry. 

If you’re at one of the frontier labs and would like to discuss making this happen, please get in touch.

item.title: CCF: Billions are coming. Still no plan to give well?
item.description:
Published on September 25, 2026 11:32 AM GMT

TLDR: Everyone’s talking about what the money could do, but few about how to decide where it goes.

This post is part of the new series of articles on cross-cause giving and the new wave of philanthropy. Stay tuned to the EA Forum and our Substack for the latest takes on topics such as giving now vs. later, common pitfalls in cause prioritization, and other crucial considerations from the Cross-Cause Fund (CCF) team at Rethink Priorities.
  
Amid all the discussion of the coming wave of AI-driven philanthropy, one question gets surprisingly little attention: how should this money be allocated across causes, and on what basis?

The stakes are large. One back-of-the-envelope calculation estimated that yearly philanthropic spending could increase by $37 billion to $100 billion, a 6–17% jump. About two-fifths of that ($15–40 billion) will likely come from Anthropic founders and employees, most of whom are likely to give in a way influenced by effective altruism, trying to maximize impact per dollar. (The remaining three-fifths might come from the OpenAI Foundation.) That is fifteen to forty times the $1 billion moved by effective giving organizations in 2024, every year.

A number of people have raised concerns about this surge in giving. Sjir Hoeijmakers is worried that the money will be spent on charities that make donors feel good, rather than on charities that most effectively improve the world. Nan Ransohoff is worried about scaling up nonprofit infrastructure to handle this much giving. Lewis Bollard is worried about negative effects on the movement culture, e.g., collaboration between nonprofits, maintaining shared values as the movement expands, and the discipline to spend each dollar in the best way to improve conditions for animals. Morgan Fairless worries that charities spend a lot of time preparing for a wave of philanthropy that never materializes.

All of these concerns are reasonable, but they sit downstream of a more fundamental one. Too often, the allocation question is answered by default: donors lean on a trusted advisor’s instincts, a cause they feel connected to, or the assumption that there will be so much money that everything worth funding will get funded anyway. Each of these is a decision about tradeoffs, made without being examined, e.g., between humans and animals, present and future generations, certain benefits and uncertain ones, giving now and giving later. A flood of money doesn’t make those tradeoffs go away. It raises the stakes of getting them wrong.

Will there be enough opportunities to fund? Spoiler: Yes.

I have seen some people argue that AI-related donations will be so large that they will saturate all effective cause areas, so we don’t need to worry about doing comparisons between different uses of the money.

First of all, this is a very flip attitude to take about human and animal lives. It amounts to saying, “it doesn’t matter if I send tens of millions of dollars to the wrong place! Eventually, someone will fund the right things. Not me, but you know, someone.”

Second, this amounts to saying that the AI-related wave of philanthropy will be sufficient to solve all world problems. I will believe this happens when it happens. The American philanthropic sector spends $600 billion every year, and yet as far as I can tell, the world still has problems. It is possible to catastrophically mismanage enormous sums of money, such that tens of millions of dollars are spent on giving a concert hall somewhat better acoustics, while opportunities to save a life for ~$3000 go unfunded. I’d argue this type of mismanagement is the norm, and is likely to continue, even among people trying to do better, without careful thought about how to allocate across different areas.

While AI-related donations will allow us to do a lot of good, their impact is likely limited. We should not prepare for extreme ambitions and unlimited resources, or as Neil Dullaghan put it, “We’re not talking about plans to absorb trillions of dollars to buy Tyson Foods and build cultivated meat on the Moon.”

Determining if there’s something left worth funding depends on thinking about tradeoffs

Whether you know it or not, when making donation decisions you are always making tradeoffs. There’s no such thing as a “saturation point” at which point important causes would no longer be able to spend money effectively, or if there is, it’s so high that we have no realistic prospect of reaching it any time soon. Even if you look at just one cause area, like Global Health, below the GiveWell top charities are charities that just barely missed their bar. Below those charities are others that are somewhat worse or more thinly evidenced. At some point, if you can’t think of anything else to do with the money within that cause, you could work with GiveDirectly to create a universal basic income for everyone in the entire world.

But you can also look more broadly. If you care about the suffering of sentient beings, the ladder doesn’t end with humans. Corporate campaigns to reduce the suffering of farmed chickens have been estimated to spare numerous hens from cage confinement per dollar, which is plausibly orders of magnitude more cost-effective, in suffering averted, than even the best global health interventions, if you’re willing to give chickens some moral consideration. Beyond chickens, there are billions of farmed fish and shrimp whose welfare receives almost no philanthropic attention. These are areas where a marginal dollar can still buy improvements so cheaply that they, too, clear cost-effectiveness bars some global health interventions can’t, assuming you give these species some moral concern. And beyond the present entirely, there are efforts to reduce catastrophic risks from engineered pandemics, nuclear war, or advanced AI, where if you believe the future might be big, the numbers at stake are so large that even small changes in probability matter enormously.

Long before any of these areas “fills up,” you’ll hit the limits of your budget. The question is never whether there’s something worth funding; it’s which of the many worthwhile things you’ll fund first.

It’s not obvious that something a few steps down from GiveWell’s funding bar deserves no money, and it’s not obvious that they deserve to be flush with cash. But if you don’t think about what you’re doing, you’re probably going to do one or the other more-or-less at random.

“Effectiveness” isn’t an on/off switch

Another issue with thinking there’s some clear saturation point after which there’s nothing to fund is that it seems to stem from a belief within the effective altruism (EA) community that, once you run out of options the community currently considers high-value, you can do whatever you want with your money. Inside or outside of EA, people often implicitly divide charities into approved (”effective”) and unapproved (”ineffective”). They see all charities that don’t currently have the stamp of approval as a homogeneous mass of Ineffective Charities. If all the Effective Charities have their funding gap filled, you can do whatever you want with the rest.

But, in reality, these charities range widely in effectiveness. Some are net-harmful, while others are as good as or better than charities currently considered “effective” by the EA movement. If you ought to spend your donations effectively, which I do think you should, then your obligation doesn’t go away when you have run out of already vetted and investigated charities. You can and should vet and investigate new charities! This assumption doesn’t make much sense, which I think is why people rarely make the argument explicitly.

Making tradeoffs between apples and oranges

Philanthropy presents a number of thorny ethical issues which we don’t know how to resolve. We don’t know how to trade off between humans and chickens, or between present people and future people, or between improved health and increased income. We don’t know how risk-averse we ought to be. We don’t know how much certainty to put into moral theories that, for example, don’t allow you to aggregate many small health benefits to be the equivalent of saving a life. We don’t know whether you should combine moral theories or go with your best guess, and if you do combine them, we don’t know how.

I’ve been talking — and many people talk about this issue — like you can line up every giving opportunity on a single scale and proceed down the list. But this is a mistake. Doing good isn’t like stock valuation or investment in a for-profit company. When you invest in a for-profit company, you know what your goal is, i.e., to earn as much money as possible. But when you do good, you don’t. Sincere people trying to improve the world as much as possible come to wildly divergent views about what the best thing to do is.

The effective altruism movement is pretty good, though not perfect, at addressing empirical uncertainty through monitoring and evaluation programs, RCTs, and charity evaluators such as GiveWell and the EA Funds. But the decisions that most change where money goes are usually not only empirical; they’re also moral. It is rarely the case that one person donates to cage-free egg campaigns and another donates to malaria net distribution because they have different reads of the empirical evidence. Instead, the person who donates to cage-free egg campaigns likely values chickens more than the person who donates to malaria net distribution, or they value the certainty of the benefit to humans less than the increased potential size of the benefits to chickens.

In order to treat doing good like a stock valuation, you have to trust that you can weigh evidence in ethics and come to a robust decision. But we aren’t that good at ethics! The evidence, in many cases, consists largely of thought experiments. You shouldn’t have the same confidence in your answers to thought experiments that you have in empirical, real-world results that you can point to.

Many people seem to assume that a flood of money solves these problems, because you can just fund everything. But you can’t realistically fund everything. A flood of money doesn’t make the problem easier; it just raises the stakes of solving it. No one has a real model of how best to spend billions of dollars, because no one has a real model of how best to spend millions or thousands of dollars.

Think you already know how to distribute effectively? What’s your actual plan?

The best way to see how unprepared we are here is to ask people what their practical plan is: what do they think the distribution of money should be and why they think it’s the best. Often, they will look blank or stutter through an explanation, making it clear they don’t yet know.

Much of the poor reasoning around the third wave of philanthropy may stem from being overwhelmed by the difficulties of making these decisions. It’s easy to give up and say that all the reasonable choices are equally good so you can give to whichever ones you feel like. However, these problems are hard, but not impossible to tackle. You can make real progress on giving in a principled way.

In my view, to give effectively, you need at least:

  • Up-to-date information about how charities you might donate to plan to spend money.
  • Up-to-date information about where other donors are spending money.
  • Accurate models of how many benefits of which kinds come from that spending.
  • A clear way of thinking about tradeoffs between different kinds of goods, including philosophically confusing concepts like moral weights, risk aversion, and aggregation of small goods.

Sometimes, we can be tempted to think that we don’t need a complex, explicit model; we’ll just use our best judgment. But any time we make a decision about how to allocate our donations, we’re, in fact, using a model, at least tacitly. Making the model explicit allows us to question and reconsider the assumptions we make, figure out which considerations actually matter for the final decision, and to learn how sensitive our conclusions are to aspects of the model we’re uncertain of. Often, if you don’t make your model explicit, your best judgment simply reflects your biases (towards humans, towards charities you have an emotional connection to, towards problems that feel vivid...).

At Rethink Priorities, we built the Cross-Cause Model, and the accompanying Cross-Cause Fund, to take these questions on directly. It brings together empirical estimates of what interventions achieve with explicit, adjustable assumptions about the hardest moral questions: how to weigh different beings, how much risk to accept, and how to act when moral theories disagree. It draws on years of research across global health, animal welfare, and catastrophic risk. It isn’t perfect, and it isn’t the only possible approach. But we believe it is currently the most comprehensive all-things-considered philanthropic tool available for allocating across causes.

Whatever approach you use, though, you need one. The more money at stake, the more it matters that your decisions rest on reasoning you can examine, question, and improve.

In the coming weeks, we plan to address various concerns about philanthropic giving, like:

  • Giving now vs. later
  • Giving in the face of new AI trajectories
  • Cause prioritization done wrong and how to prevent it
  • How to avoid giving disasters
  • And many more.

Stay tuned.

At Rethink Priorities, we built the Cross-Cause Model, and the accompanying Cross-Cause Fund, to take these questions on directly. It brings together empirical estimates of what interventions achieve with explicit, adjustable assumptions about the hardest moral questions: how to weigh different beings, how much risk to accept, and how to act when moral theories disagree. It draws on years of research across global health, animal welfare, and catastrophic risk. It isn’t perfect, and it isn’t the only possible approach. But we believe it is currently the most comprehensive all-things-considered philanthropic tool available for allocating across causes.

Whatever approach you use, though, you need one. The more money at stake, the more it matters that your decisions rest on reasoning you can examine, question, and improve.

  • Giving now vs. later
  • Giving in the face of new AI trajectories
  • Cause prioritization done wrong and how to prevent it
  • How to avoid giving disasters
